extracted.intended_audience: federal agency economists and analysts preparing regulatory benefit-cost analyses (BCA)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for conducting benefit-cost analysis for federal regulations, including how to treat uncertainty, risk preferences, and how to choose and estimate discount rates (SRTP).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume risk neutrality by default
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed revisions remove the general statement that an assumption of risk-neutrality is generally appropriate and acknowledge risk aversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Risk aversion is widespread and consistent with common models of rational preferences; however, there are circumstances where assuming risk neutrality may be reasonable (e.g., when a regulation has modest effects on each person or group, when net benefits are almost identical across states of the world, or when people are fully insured or could choose to be). If evidence shows risk-neutral or risk-seeking behavior in the relevant context, analyses should alter assumptions accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculate certainty-equivalent valuations for uncertain costs and benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should calculate certainty-equivalent values for uncertain costs and benefits rather than relying solely on expected surplus estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB provides additional mathematical detail in the final Circular A-4 on how to perform certainty-equivalent calculations. The use of certainty-equivalents and comparison with risk-adjusted discount rates is discussed further in 'Accounting for Risk When Discounting.' Certainty-equivalent approaches can lead to estimates that are conceptually sound and materially different, especially when individuals face large uninsurable risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide quantitative analysis of uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative approaches to the analysis of uncertainty are valuable and should be used rather than rejected out of hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB disagrees with commenters who were critical of quantitative methods; such approaches can shed light on the welfare effects of regulatory alternatives. Where practical, agencies should employ quantitative methods to account for uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a descriptive (market-based) approach to discounting in many circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Circular A-4 recommends a descriptive approach to discounting—using observable market rates—because it enables policymakers to base allocations on the tradeoffs society actually makes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize this reflects one strand of the literature; prescriptive approaches addressing intergenerational ethical concerns may be appropriate in some contexts. The descriptive approach is primarily justified because financial-market rates are real prices at which consumption can be traded over time and provide an objective evidentiary basis for parameters used in policymaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider prescriptive approaches for intergenerational ethical issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Special ethical considerations arise when comparing benefits and costs across generations, and some literature uses a prescriptive approach to long-term discounting to weight future generations' welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While OMB generally recommends a descriptive approach, agencies should recognize ethical arguments for prescriptive discounting when deciding how to treat long-term intergenerational effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate the Social Rate of Time Preference (SRTP) using real returns on long-duration U.S. government debt
rubrics_metrics.description: One approach assumes the real (inflation-adjusted) rate of return on long-term U.S. government debt provides a fair approximation of the SRTP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For simplicity, transparency, and tractability, Circular A-4 adopts this approach and uses one default SRTP for effects from the present through 30 years. OMB retained the 2003 method and updated the averaging period; where available, use TIPS for years after its introduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer TIPS returns to Treasuries when available to estimate SRTP
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) return data for years after TIPS introduction to avoid combining ex-ante returns with ex-post inflation measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TIPS offers protection against inflation risk by indexing principal to CPI inflation; using TIPS avoids the inconsistency of using 10-year Treasury notes with CPI for inflation measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use returns on capital as the default SRTP proxy
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the rate of return on capital assumes the opportunity cost of regulatory benefits/costs is capital investment, but capital returns include risk premiums and reflect market distortions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capital investment is much riskier than nearly risk-free government debt; the higher yield reflects compensation for additional risk (risk premium) and may reflect returns to market power, externalities, and other distortions. Some regulation effects are best modeled as falling on consumption rather than capital; a discount rate appropriate for certainty-equivalent benefits should not include a risk premium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using consumer-behavior-based high discount rate estimates to infer SRTP
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence from choices like military personnel pay selection, used-car purchasers, or durable goods yielding very high discount rates are not appropriate bases for SRTP estimation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such studies may suffer from omission bias and capture behavioral biases, information asymmetries, or other factors rather than true time preferences. OMB is concerned these analyses do not adequately capture all relevant factors and therefore are not appropriate for SRTP estimation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use high-interest consumer debt rates (credit cards, payday loans, mortgages) to estimate SRTP
rubrics_metrics.description: High consumer interest rates are risk-inclusive and reflect default risk and lenders' risk premiums rather than a pure social rate of time preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rates include components for default probability and risk premium; they are not suitable guides to SRTP because they conflate default risk and other services (e.g., liquidity) with time preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate bond yields add little beyond Treasury yields for SRTP estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: High-grade non-Treasury bond yields vary with default risk and largely reflect risk premia; they do not provide additional relevant insight beyond long-duration government bond yields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variation in corporate yields is driven by the riskiness of included instruments and time-varying risk premia; thus corporate yields are not preferable to Treasuries for SRTP estimation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about making many micro-adjustments to SRTP (liquidity premia, term premia, default risk, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters suggested adjustments (behavioral biases, zero lower bound, liquidity premia, term premia, default risk, taxation of income on Federal debt) that could lower or raise SRTP, but OMB generally finds attempting most adjustments not worth the potential for error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB acknowledges the potential for upward bias in its SRTP estimate from these considerations but concludes most adjustments risk introducing error. An appropriate adjustment for inflation raised the proposed SRTP estimate from 1.7% to 2.0%.

rubrics_metrics.name: When it is reasonable to ignore risk preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Risk preferences may be ignored when a regulation’s effects are modest per person, net benefits are nearly identical across states of the world, or when people are fully insured (unless transaction costs of insurance are substantial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB noted these as common circumstances where assuming risk neutrality is reasonable; analysts should evaluate materiality of risk-preference incorporation on a case-by-case basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish risk aversion from behavioral biases like loss aversion and ambiguity aversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Risk aversion (concave utility in standard theory) is a standard, rational preference feature and should not be conflated with behavioral biases such as loss aversion or ambiguity aversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB clarifies that some commenters conflated loss aversion with risk aversion; analyses should treat risk aversion as consistent with utility maximization while separately addressing behavioral biases where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide mathematical clarity so agencies can calculate benefits under different risk assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB added mathematical detail in the final Circular to guide calculation of certainty-equivalent valuations and benefits under differing risk assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This additional detail aims to help agencies compute benefits and costs under alternative risk assumptions and to alleviate concerns about how to perform such calculations in practice.
